title: Set Operations and Set Identities
quickIdea: Every set identity is proved the same way: take an arbitrary element of the left side, rewrite membership step by step, and land on the right side. Do it in both directions for equality.
remember: Union, intersection, difference and complement are all defined by membership: x in A union B means x in A or x in B; x in A minus B means x in A and x not in B.
The symmetric difference A triangle B is (A minus B) union (B minus A): the elements in exactly one of the two sets.
De Morgan within a universe U: the complement of A union B is the intersection of the complements, and the complement of A intersect B is the union of the complements.
Distributive laws: A intersect (B union C) = (A intersect B) union (A intersect C), and the dual with union outside.
To prove X subset Y, take an arbitrary element x of X and derive x in Y. To prove X = Y, do this in both directions.
A minus B and B minus A are different sets in general; they are equal only when A = B.
A minus B = A intersect (complement of B), which is why the identities for difference follow from De Morgan.
The cardinality of a union is not the sum of cardinalities unless the sets are disjoint; |A union B| = |A| + |B| - |A intersect B| is proved in the combinatorics inclusion-exclusion card.
Membership proofs never need a Venn diagram; a diagram only suggests which identity to try.

example.prompt: Prove that the complement of A union B equals the intersection of the complements, inside a universe U.
example.work: Take x in U. Then x is in the complement of A union B exactly when x is not in A union B, which holds exactly when x is not in A and x is not in B, which holds exactly when x is in the complement of A and in the complement of B, that is x is in the intersection of the complements. Every step is an equivalence, so both inclusions hold at once.
example.answer: The two sets contain the same elements, so they are equal. This is De Morgan's law for sets, and its dual for intersection is proved the same way.

gateAngle: Set identities are rarely asked as a bare identity; they appear as the first step of a counting question or of a relation question, and the option that survives is the one that respects De Morgan.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: U = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, A = {1, 2, 3}, B = {3, 4}. Compute A union B, A intersect B, A minus B, B minus A and the symmetric difference.
variations.answer: A union B = {1, 2, 3, 4}; A intersect B = {3}; A minus B = {1, 2}; B minus A = {4}; symmetric difference = {1, 2, 4}.
variations.why: Each operation is read off the membership definition; the symmetric difference is the union of the two differences, so it holds exactly the elements in one set but not both.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: Is it true that (A minus B) union B = A for all sets A and B? Justify.
variations.answer: No. The identity that always holds is (A minus B) union B = A union B.
variations.why: Elements of B that are not in A appear on the left but not on the right. With A = {1} and B = {2} the left side is {1, 2} and the right side is {1}.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: Simplify (A union B) intersect (A union complement of B).
variations.why: Distribute the union over the intersection: (A union B) intersect (A union B complement) = A union (B intersect B complement) = A union empty = A. This is the absorption pattern GATE hides inside simplification questions.

trap.what: Applying De Morgan with the wrong connective, or assuming difference commutes.
trap.why: The complement turns union into intersection and intersection into union; keeping the same connective is the single most common error. Difference is not symmetric because membership in the first set is required.
trap.counterexample: U = {1, 2, 3}, A = {1}, B = {2}. The complement of A union B is {3}, while the union of the complements is {2, 3} union {1, 3} = {1, 2, 3}. The two differ, so the wrong De Morgan is visibly false.

check.question: |A| = 5, |B| = 4 and |A intersect B| = 2. Give |A union B| and the cardinality of the symmetric difference.
check.answer: |A union B| = 7 and the symmetric difference has 5 elements.
check.explanation: Inclusion-exclusion gives 5 + 4 - 2 = 7. The symmetric difference holds the 3 elements of A only and the 2 elements of B only, so 5 in total.
